short: Testing a trading or investing strategy on past market data to see how it would have performed, before risking real money.
kid: Before playing a new board game for real, you try your plan on old games to see if it would have won. A plan that only wins old games may still lose tomorrow.
detail: Backtesting runs a clearly defined set of rules (what to buy, when to sell, how much to hold) through historical prices and data, and records the trades, returns, drawdowns and costs the strategy would have produced. It is the standard first check for quant strategies, factor portfolios and trading systems. A useful backtest uses only data that was available on each past date, includes stocks that were later delisted, deducts brokerage, taxes, slippage and impact costs, and checks periods the rules were not designed on. The common confusion is treating a good backtest as proof: a pattern can be an accident found by trying many variations, and markets change. A backtest shows a strategy could have worked, not that it will. Many retail algo and model-portfolio platforms in India show backtested charts; these are hypothetical results that nobody actually earned.
example: Say a backtest shows a strategy earning 15% a year before costs while trading 40 times a year. If each trade costs 0.25% of the portfolio, costs total 40 x 0.25% = 10% a year, so the realistic return falls to roughly 5%.

short: Building a model or strategy so closely around past data that it captures random noise and then fails on new data.
kid: If you pass a spelling test by remembering the order of the answers, you get full marks on that test. On a new test, you are lost.
detail: Overfitting happens when a model has so many rules, settings or tweaks relative to the data that it explains past ups and downs perfectly, including pure luck, but has no real power to predict. In finance it usually comes from data snooping: testing hundreds of indicators, look-back windows or stock filters and keeping whichever looked best. With enough tries something will look brilliant by chance, the same problem as p-hacking in research. Warning signs are a very high backtested Sharpe ratio, many finely tuned settings and results that collapse when one setting changes slightly. Defences include out-of-sample and walk-forward testing, simpler models, stricter significance thresholds that allow for the number of trials, and demanding an economic reason for the pattern. Overfitting is not the same as look-ahead bias: an overfit model can use only legitimate past data and still fail.
example: Say an analyst tests 100 trading rules that have no real edge. At a 5% significance level, about 100 x 0.05 = 5 of them will still look statistically significant purely by chance, and the best of those is likely to disappoint in live trading.

short: An error in testing a strategy where it uses information that would not actually have been available at the time of the decision.
kid: It is like guessing who wins a race after peeking at the finish line. Your guess looks perfect, but only because you looked ahead.
detail: Look-ahead bias creeps into a backtest or study when the data used to make a decision on a given date includes facts that became known only later. Classic causes: using a company's annual results as of the financial year-end when they were actually published weeks later, using revised GDP or inflation figures instead of the first release, using today's index members for past years, or trading at a day's closing price on a signal calculated from that same close. Because the strategy secretly knows the future, returns look far better than anything achievable. In India, under SEBI's listing rules as of 2025, companies get up to 45 days after a quarter ends to publish results and 60 days after the financial year ends for annual results, so a test must lag accounting data accordingly. The fix is point-in-time data that records what was known, and when.
example: Say ABC Ltd's results for the year to 31 March 2024 were released on 20 May 2024. A backtest that buys ABC on 1 April 2024 because those results showed strong profit growth is using information nobody had for another 49 days.

short: The error of studying only the winners that still exist, such as funds or companies, while ignoring the ones that failed or disappeared.
kid: If you only count the sandcastles still standing at the end of the day, you will think sandcastles are very strong. You forgot all the ones the waves knocked down.
detail: Survivorship bias arises when a sample includes only those that survived to the end of the period, so failures are invisible and averages look better than reality. Mutual fund databases are the classic case: schemes that did badly are often merged into others or closed, and their records drop out, lifting the average return of the funds still visible. The same happens when a backtest uses today's Nifty 50 or Sensex members for past years, because companies that collapsed or were removed are missing, while later winners are included before they won. In India, SEBI's 2017 scheme recategorisation led to many fund mergers, a reminder to check whether category averages include merged schemes. The fix is a survivorship-free dataset that keeps delisted stocks and defunct funds. The bias also distorts stories: studying only successful founders exaggerates what their habits explain.
example: Say 100 funds launch together and 20 are shut after poor results. If the 80 survivors averaged 12% a year and the 20 closed funds averaged 2%, the true average across all 100 was (80 x 12 + 20 x 2) / 100 = 10%, not the 12% a survivors-only database shows.

short: A model that explains an investment's returns by how strongly it responds to a few shared drivers, such as the market, company size or value.
kid: A cake's taste comes mostly from a few things: sugar, butter and flour. If you know how much of each went in, you can guess most of how it will taste.
detail: A factor model splits an asset's return into parts explained by common factors plus a leftover part specific to that asset. The general form is a regression: return = alpha + sum of (factor exposure x factor return) + error. The simplest is the single-factor market model, where the only factor is the market return and the exposure is beta, as in the CAPM. Multi-factor models add drivers that can be macroeconomic (inflation, interest rates, oil), fundamental (size, value, momentum, quality) or purely statistical. Fund managers use them to see what really drives a portfolio, to separate skill (alpha) from factor exposure, to hedge and to estimate risk; commercial risk models such as MSCI's Barra models are factor models. A common confusion: a factor that explains returns well need not earn a premium, and an exposure (beta) is not the same as an expected profit.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a market beta of 1.2 and a value exposure of 0.5, with zero alpha. In a month when the market returns 2% and the value factor returns 1%, the model predicts 1.2 x 2% + 0.5 x 1% = 2.9%; if ABC actually returned 3.5%, the unexplained 0.6% is stock-specific.
formula: R_i = alpha_i + b_i1 x F_1 + b_i2 x F_2 + ... + b_ik x F_k + e_i

short: A model explaining stock returns with three drivers: the overall market, the extra return of small companies and the extra return of cheap value stocks.
kid: To guess how tall a plant will grow, you look at three things: sunshine, the size of its pot and the kind of seed. Three clues guess better than one.
detail: Proposed by Eugene Fama and Kenneth French in 1993, the model extends the CAPM by adding two factors to the market: SMB (small minus big), the return of small-cap stocks minus large-caps, and HML (high minus low), the return of high book-to-market (value) stocks minus low book-to-market (growth) stocks. Regressing a fund's returns on the three factors shows whether its performance came from tilts towards small or cheap stocks rather than stock-picking skill. In 2015 they added profitability (RMW) and investment (CMA) to form the five-factor model, while Mark Carhart's 1997 four-factor model adds momentum. Researchers at IIM Ahmedabad publish Fama-French style factor data for Indian stocks. Confusion to avoid: the factors describe where returns came from; whether the size and value premiums will persist is still debated.
example: Say a fund's regression gives a market beta of 1.0, an SMB loading of 0.4 and an HML loading of 0.3, with alpha near zero. If in a year the market beat the risk-free rate by 8%, SMB returned 5% and HML 4%, the model expects an excess return of 1.0 x 8% + 0.4 x 5% + 0.3 x 4% = 11.2%, so an 11% excess return shows no real skill.
formula: R_i - R_f = alpha + b x (R_m - R_f) + s x SMB + h x HML + e

short: A theory that an asset's expected return depends on how strongly it reacts to several broad economic forces, each with its own reward for risk.
kid: A farmer's harvest depends on rain, sunshine and wind. A crop that gets hurt more by bad weather has to promise a bigger harvest before anyone will plant it.
detail: Developed by Stephen Ross in 1976, arbitrage pricing theory says an asset's expected return equals the risk-free rate plus the sum of its exposures (betas) to several systematic factors, each multiplied by that factor's risk premium. Factors are often macroeconomic, such as surprises in inflation, industrial production, credit spreads or oil prices. The logic is no-arbitrage: if two well-diversified portfolios had the same factor exposures but different expected returns, traders could buy one and sell the other for a riskless profit, pushing prices back into line. Unlike the CAPM, APT does not assume everyone holds the market portfolio or that only one risk matters, so it is more flexible, but it does not say which factors to use or how many. Confusion to avoid: APT is a pricing theory; a factor model is the statistical tool used to apply it.
example: Say a portfolio has a beta of 1.5 to inflation surprises and 0.8 to industrial-production growth, with factor premiums of 2% and 3%. With a risk-free rate of 6%, APT gives an expected return of 6% + 1.5 x 2% + 0.8 x 3% = 11.4%.
formula: E(R_i) = R_f + b_i1 x RP_1 + b_i2 x RP_2 + ... + b_ik x RP_k

short: The tendency of cheap stocks, priced low compared with their profits or net assets, to earn higher long-run returns than expensive ones.
kid: Toys on the sale shelf are often fine, just unloved for now. Buying them cheaply and waiting can work out better than paying top price for the toy everyone wants.
detail: The value premium is the historical extra return of value stocks (high book-to-market, low price-to-earnings) over growth stocks (low book-to-market, high P/E). In the Fama-French model it is measured by HML, high minus low book-to-market. Explanations split two ways: risk-based (cheap firms are often weak and suffer in recessions, so investors demand compensation) and behavioural (investors over-extrapolate bad news, overpricing glamour stocks and underpricing unloved ones). The premium is not steady: US value stocks lagged growth for much of 2010 to 2020, prompting debate about whether book value understates companies built on intangible assets. In India, factor indices such as the Nifty50 Value 20 give access to the style. Confusion to avoid: the factor is a statistical long-short spread, while value investing is a broader, judgement-based philosophy.
example: Say over a year a portfolio of the cheapest 30% of stocks by price-to-book returns 16% and a portfolio of the most expensive 30% returns 11%. The value premium, or HML, for that year is 16% - 11% = 5 percentage points.
formula: HML = Return of high book-to-market portfolio - Return of low book-to-market portfolio

short: The historical tendency of small companies' shares to earn higher average returns than large companies' shares, as a reward for extra risk.
kid: A tiny new lemonade stand might close or might grow big, while the giant stall is steady. People who back the tiny stands want a bigger reward for taking the chance.
detail: The size premium, measured in the Fama-French model as SMB (small minus big), is the extra return small-cap stocks have earned over large-caps, first documented by Rolf Banz in 1981. Proposed reasons include higher business risk, weaker access to finance, lower liquidity and thinner analyst coverage. Evidence since its discovery is mixed: in the US the premium weakened after the early 1980s, and much of it sits in tiny, illiquid stocks and in January, where trading costs bite. It looks stronger after controlling for quality, since junky small firms drag it down. Under SEBI's mutual fund categorisation as of 2025, large-caps are the top 100 companies by market value, mid-caps 101 to 250 and small-caps 251 onwards, and Indian small-cap indices have seen long stretches of both outperformance and steep falls. Do not read the premium as guaranteed: it comes with much higher volatility.
example: Say over a year a portfolio of small companies returns 18% and one of large companies returns 12%, so SMB is 18% - 12% = 6 percentage points. If next year small returns 2% and large 9%, SMB is -7 points, showing how unstable the premium is.
formula: SMB = Average return of small-cap portfolios - Average return of large-cap portfolios

short: The finding that steadier, less volatile stocks have historically earned returns as good as or better than riskier ones, against what theory predicts.
kid: You might think the wildest roller coaster wins the biggest prize. But often the calm, steady ride ends up giving you just as much, with fewer tummy flips.
detail: Standard theory such as the CAPM says higher-beta, riskier stocks should earn higher average returns. Across many markets the opposite has often held: low-volatility and low-beta stocks have delivered similar or higher returns with smaller swings, so their risk-adjusted returns are much better. Explanations include borrowing limits (investors who cannot use leverage buy high-beta stocks to get more market exposure, overpricing them), a taste for lottery-like stocks, and fund managers judged against benchmarks who avoid dull stocks. Investors access the effect through minimum-volatility and low-vol indices and funds, such as those tracking the Nifty100 Low Volatility 30 index. Caveats: low-vol portfolios tilt towards defensive sectors like consumer staples and utilities, can lag badly in sharp rallies, and become expensive when crowded. Low volatility does not mean no risk of loss.
example: Say over five years a low-volatility portfolio returns 13% a year with 12% volatility and a high-volatility portfolio returns 12% a year with 28% volatility. With a 6% risk-free rate, the Sharpe ratios are (13 - 6) / 12 = 0.58 and (12 - 6) / 28 = 0.21, so the calmer portfolio earned far more per unit of risk.

short: A factor and investing style favouring financially strong companies with high, stable profits and low debt, which have historically earned extra returns.
kid: When picking apples, you choose the shiny, firm ones without bruises. Strong, healthy apples tend to last longer than soft ones.
detail: The quality factor captures the tendency of profitable, stable, conservatively financed companies to outperform weaker ones over time. There is no single definition: index providers combine measures such as return on equity, gross profitability, earnings stability, low leverage and accruals (how much reported profit is backed by cash). Robert Novy-Marx showed in 2013 that gross profitability predicts returns, and Fama and French added a profitability factor, RMW (robust minus weak), in their 2015 five-factor model. Quality often holds up better in downturns, acting as a defensive tilt, and it pairs well with value because cheap stocks that are also high quality are less likely to be value traps. In India, index funds track indices such as the Nifty200 Quality 30. Confusion to avoid: a great company is not automatically a good investment; quality stocks can be so expensive that future returns disappoint.
example: Say a screen keeps companies with return on equity above 20% and debt-to-equity below 0.5. ABC Ltd, with net profit of ₹200 crore on average equity of ₹800 crore (ROE of 25%) and debt of ₹240 crore (0.3 times equity), passes; XYZ Ltd, with ROE of 12%, fails.

short: The tendency of assets that have risen most over the past several months to keep outperforming, and recent losers to keep lagging, for a while.
kid: A ball rolling down a hill tends to keep rolling the same way for a bit. Things that are going up often keep going up for a little while before they slow down.
detail: In factor investing, momentum is the finding, documented by Narasimhan Jegadeesh and Sheridan Titman in 1993, that stocks with the highest returns over the past 3 to 12 months tend to beat those with the lowest over the next 3 to 12 months. A standard measure is the past 12-month return excluding the latest month, because very short-term returns tend to reverse. The factor, often called WML (winners minus losers) or UMD, appears across stocks, sectors, currencies, commodities and countries. Explanations are mostly behavioural: investors underreact to news, then herd. Momentum has strong long-run returns but suffers rare, violent crashes, as in 2009 when beaten-down stocks rebounded sharply. In India, funds track indices such as the Nifty200 Momentum 30. Confusion to avoid: factor momentum ranks stocks against each other over months, unlike a news headline saying the market has momentum.
example: Say on 1 January you rank 200 stocks by their return from the start of last January to the end of November, skipping December. You buy the top 20% (40 stocks) and avoid the bottom 40; if the winners then return 15% and the losers 6% over the next year, the momentum spread is 15% - 6% = 9 percentage points.
formula: 12-1 momentum score = (Price 1 month ago / Price 12 months ago) - 1

short: The tendency of a price, return or ratio that has moved far from its long-run average to drift back towards that average over time.
kid: If you stretch a rubber band far, it snaps back towards the middle. Some things that wander far away tend to come back to where they usually are.
detail: Mean reversion describes a series that is pulled back towards a long-run level after moving away from it, so large gaps tend to shrink. It shows up in interest-rate spreads, in volatility (which spikes in crises and then settles), in valuation ratios such as P/E and in the price gap between closely related assets. Stocks show short-term reversal over days to a month and some long-horizon reversal over three to five years, while momentum dominates in between. Mean-reversion strategies buy what has fallen unusually far below its average and sell what has risen far above, as in pairs trading. Two cautions: the mean itself can shift permanently, as when a company's business changes, and a random walk has no mean to return to, so a stock that has fallen is not automatically due to bounce. Regression to the mean explains why star fund managers often look ordinary the next year.
example: Say a stock's P/E has averaged 20 over ten years and now stands at 30. A mean-reversion view expects it to drift back towards 20; if earnings stay flat, that implies a price fall of (30 - 20) / 30, or about 33%.
formula: dX = theta x (mu - X) x dt + sigma x dW (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; theta = speed of reversion, mu = long-run mean)

short: A strategy that buys one of two closely related stocks and sells the other when their usual price relationship stretches, betting it will snap back.
kid: Two friends usually walk side by side. If one runs ahead, you bet they will soon be side by side again, whichever one moves.
detail: Pairs trading is a market-neutral strategy built on two securities whose prices normally move together, such as two large private banks. The trader tracks the spread or price ratio between them; when it moves unusually far from its average, often a z-score of 2 or more, the trader buys the relatively cheap one and short sells the expensive one, closing both when the gap narrows. Because one leg is long and the other short, broad market moves largely cancel out. Rigorous versions test for cointegration, a statistical sign that the gap is genuinely stable rather than merely correlated. The big risk is a broken relationship: a merger, fraud or rule change can widen the gap for good. In India, the short leg is commonly taken through single-stock futures, since under the rules as of 2025 an overnight cash-market short needs shares borrowed through securities lending and borrowing (SLB).
example: Say stocks A and B usually trade at a price ratio of 2.0, and today A is ₹420 and B is ₹200, a ratio of 2.1. A trader shorts 100 A and buys 210 B (₹42,000 each side). If the ratio returns to 2.0 with A at ₹410 and B at ₹205, the profit is 100 x ₹10 + 210 x ₹5 = ₹2,050 before costs.
formula: Spread z-score = (Current spread - Average spread) / Standard deviation of spread

short: A quant strategy that trades many securities at once, using statistical models to profit from small, temporary mispricings that tend to correct.
kid: Imagine a hundred tiny guesses that are each right a little more often than wrong. One guess means little, but together they add up to a small win.
detail: Statistical arbitrage, or stat arb, extends pairs trading to hundreds or thousands of securities. Models estimate where each stock should trade relative to related stocks, sectors or factors, then buy those that look temporarily cheap and short those that look expensive, keeping the portfolio roughly neutral to the market and to industry and factor exposures. Each position has only a slight edge, so profits depend on diversification, high turnover and tight cost control, which is why stat arb is run by quant hedge funds and proprietary trading firms with strong technology. Despite the name it is not true arbitrage: there is no locked-in, riskless profit, and losses can be large when many funds hold similar positions and rush to exit together, as in the August 2007 quant quake. In India such strategies run in the cash and derivatives segments, subject to SEBI's algorithmic trading rules.
example: Say a stat-arb book holds 200 long and 200 short positions of ₹5 lakh each, so ₹10 crore a side and ₹20 crore gross. Earning 0.02% a day on that gross exposure gives ₹40,000 a day before costs; if trading costs take 0.005% a day (₹10,000), net profit falls to ₹30,000.

short: The idea that price changes are unpredictable, each step independent of the last, so past prices cannot reliably forecast future ones.
kid: Flip a coin to choose each step: heads you step left, tails you step right. Knowing your last steps does not help you guess the next one.
detail: In finance, the random walk hypothesis says successive price changes are independent and unpredictable, so tomorrow's move is like a coin toss, possibly with a small upward drift. It was popularised by Burton Malkiel's 1973 book A Random Walk Down Wall Street and is closely tied to weak-form market efficiency: if prices follow a random walk, chart patterns and past-price rules should not earn extra returns after costs. Statistically, a random walk is non-stationary and has no fixed mean, so shocks are permanent and the range of possible prices widens with time, which is why volatility scales with the square root of time. Evidence is mixed: momentum and short-term reversal are small departures from it. Confusion to avoid: random does not mean the market is irrational or that prices cannot trend; it means changes cannot be forecast from past prices alone.
example: Say a stock at ₹100 moves up or down ₹1 each day with equal chance. After 100 days its expected price is still ₹100, but the standard deviation of where it ends up is ₹1 x the square root of 100, or ₹10, and the path gives no clue about day 101.
formula: P_t = P_(t-1) + drift + e_t, where e_t is an unpredictable random shock

short: The theory that market prices quickly reflect all available information, so consistently beating the market after costs and risk is extremely hard.
kid: If everyone in class already knows where the hidden sweets are, you cannot get there first just by being clever. The easy treats get found straight away.
detail: Formalised by Eugene Fama in 1970, the efficient market hypothesis holds that prices fully reflect available information. It comes in three forms. Weak form: prices reflect all past prices and volumes, so technical analysis cannot earn excess returns. Semi-strong form: prices also reflect all public information such as results, announcements and news, so analysing public data cannot either. Strong form: prices reflect even private information, which the profits from insider trading show is not fully true. The practical upshot is that most active funds struggle to beat low-cost index funds after fees, a pattern S&P's SPIVA scorecards report for both the US and India. Critics point to bubbles, anomalies such as momentum, and behavioural biases. Confusion to avoid: efficiency does not mean prices are always right or that nobody ever wins; it means mispricings are hard to find and exploit consistently after costs and risk.
example: Say ABC Ltd announces at 2 pm that its profit doubled, and its share price jumps from ₹500 to ₹560, a 12% rise, within a minute. An investor who reads the news at 2:30 pm and buys at ₹560 gains nothing from it, because the information is already in the price, as semi-strong efficiency predicts.

short: Patterns where average stock returns seem to differ by time of year, month or week, such as the January effect or the Monday effect.
kid: Some days the ice cream van seems to sell more, like Fridays. But when you look closely, the pattern often fades once everyone notices it.
detail: Calendar anomalies are return patterns tied to dates rather than news. The best known are the January effect (US small-cap stocks historically outperformed in January, often linked to year-end tax-loss selling and its reversal), the Monday or weekend effect (lower average returns from Friday's close to Monday's close), the turn-of-the-month effect (stronger returns around the last and first few trading days of a month) and pre-holiday effects. In India, researchers have studied patterns around Diwali and Muhurat trading and around the April start of the financial year. Most such patterns have weakened or vanished after being published, are small relative to trading costs, and may be products of data mining across many possible dates. They matter mainly as tests of market efficiency and as a warning: a pattern that looks reliable in old data is not automatically a strategy that works.
example: Say a study finds Monday returns averaged -0.05% and other days +0.08%. On a ₹10 lakh position, the 0.13 percentage-point gap is worth ₹1,300 per Monday, but a round-trip trading cost of 0.15% (₹1,500) would wipe it out.

short: Returns measured as the natural logarithm of ending price divided by starting price, so returns over back-to-back periods simply add up.
kid: If you go up three stairs and then down three stairs, you are back where you started. Measuring this way, the ups and downs cancel out neatly.
detail: A log return, or continuously compounded return, is ln(P1 / P0), the natural logarithm of the price relative. Its key property is additivity: the log return over a month equals the sum of the daily log returns, whereas simple returns must be compounded by multiplying (1 + r) terms. Log returns are also symmetric: a rise from ₹100 to ₹200 is +0.693 and a fall back to ₹100 is -0.693, while simple returns show +100% and -50%. Quants use them widely, and option models such as Black-Scholes assume log returns are normally distributed. For small moves the two measures are nearly equal, since ln(1 + r) is close to r, but they diverge for large moves. Confusion to avoid: a portfolio's log return is not the weighted average of its assets' log returns, so use simple returns when combining assets and log returns when combining time periods.
example: Say a stock goes from ₹100 to ₹110 and then back to ₹100. The simple returns are +10% and -9.09%, which do not cancel, while the log returns are ln(1.10) = +0.0953 and ln(100 / 110) = -0.0953, which sum to exactly zero.
formula: Log return = ln(P_t / P_(t-1)) = ln(1 + simple return)

short: Converting a return or volatility measured over another period, such as a day or a month, into an equivalent yearly figure for comparison.
kid: If you save one coin every week, you can work out how many coins that makes in a whole year. Then you can compare with a friend who counts coins each month.
detail: Annualisation puts numbers from different time spans on a common yearly basis. For returns, the correct method compounds: a return r earned over a period that occurs N times a year annualises to (1 + r)^N - 1, so 1% a month becomes about 12.7% a year, not 12%. For a multi-year holding, the annualised return is the CAGR. Volatility scales differently: if returns are independent, variance grows in line with time, so annual volatility equals periodic volatility multiplied by the square root of the number of periods per year (about 252 trading days or 12 months). Annualising very short results is risky: a 3% gain in one week does not make a 300%-plus year likely. Indian mutual fund factsheets typically quote returns for periods above one year as compounded annualised (CAGR) figures. Confusion to avoid: multiplying a monthly return by 12 gives a simple, not compounded, annual rate.
example: Say a fund returns 2% in a month with monthly volatility of 4%. Compounded, the annualised return is 1.02^12 - 1 = 26.8%, and the annualised volatility is 4% x the square root of 12 = 13.9%.
formula: Annualised return = (1 + r)^N - 1, where r is the return per period and N is periods per year; Annualised volatility = Periodic volatility x sqrt(N)

short: The way ups and downs reduce long-run compounded growth, so an investment grows more slowly than its average yearly return suggests.
kid: If your sandcastle loses half its sand and then grows by half, it ends up smaller than when you started. Big wobbles make it harder to grow.
detail: Volatility drag, or variance drain, is the gap between the arithmetic average of periodic returns and the geometric (compounded) growth rate an investor actually earns. Losses hurt more than equal gains help: after a 50% fall you need a 100% gain to break even. A handy approximation is geometric return = arithmetic return - variance / 2, so a portfolio averaging 10% a year with 30% volatility compounds at only about 10% - 0.30^2 / 2 = 5.5%. The drag explains why leveraged and inverse ETFs, which reset daily, can lose value over time in choppy markets even if the index ends flat, and why steadier portfolios can compound better than their average returns suggest. It also underlies the benefit of diversification and rebalancing. Confusion to avoid: a fund quoting a high average annual return may have a much lower CAGR, so always compare compounded figures.
example: Say ₹1,00,000 gains 50% in year one and loses 50% in year two. The average annual return is 0%, but the money goes to ₹1,50,000 and then to ₹75,000, a 25% loss, or a compounded rate of about -13.4% a year.
formula: Geometric return = Arithmetic mean return - Variance / 2 (approximately)

short: Investing that uses data, mathematical models and computer-run rules, rather than individual judgement calls, to choose and manage investments.
kid: Instead of picking toys by how they feel, you follow a written list of rules, like picking the ones most friends liked this week. A helper machine follows the list for you.
detail: Quantitative or systematic investing builds portfolios from explicit, testable rules applied by computer across large numbers of securities. A typical quant process gathers data (prices, financial statements, alternative data), builds signals such as value, momentum or quality, combines them in a model, constructs a portfolio that controls risk and trading costs, and executes the trades, often algorithmically. Strategies range from slow-moving factor and smart-beta funds to statistical arbitrage and high-frequency trading. Strengths are discipline, breadth and the ability to test ideas on history; weaknesses are dependence on past patterns, overfitting, and crowding when many quants hold similar trades. Well-known quant firms include Renaissance Technologies, Two Sigma and AQR. In India, factor index funds and quant-labelled mutual fund schemes have grown alongside algo trading. Confusion to avoid: quant is a method, not a style, and a fund house's name alone does not tell you how it invests.
example: Say a hypothetical quant fund ranks the 500 largest Indian stocks each quarter on the average of their value and momentum ranks, and holds the top 50 in equal weights. With ₹100 crore, each holding gets ₹100 crore / 50 = ₹2 crore, and any stock that falls out of the top 50 is sold by rule, not by opinion.

short: Non-traditional information investors use for an edge, such as satellite images, card spending, web traffic or app downloads, beyond financial statements and prices.
kid: To guess how busy a shop is, you could count the cars outside instead of waiting for the owner to tell you. It is a clever, early clue.
detail: Alternative data covers any dataset outside the traditional sources of prices, company filings, analyst estimates and official statistics. Examples include satellite photos of car parks, ports and crop fields, aggregated card and digital-payment transactions, web-scraped prices, job postings, app usage, shipping and flight trackers, and sentiment drawn from news and social media. Hedge funds and quant managers use it to estimate company sales or economic activity before official releases. In India, analysts also track high-frequency indicators such as GST e-way bills, electricity demand and vehicle registrations, many of which are public. The challenges are cost, short histories that make backtests unreliable, messy data that needs heavy cleaning, and legal limits: data must not contain material non-public information or personal data collected without consent, an area covered by India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Signals also fade as more funds buy the same feed.
example: Say satellite counts show cars at the stores of a hypothetical ABC Retail Ltd up 12% year on year in a quarter, while analysts expect sales growth of only 5%. A fund that trusts the data buys before results; if reported sales then grow 11%, the early signal paid off.

short: A measure of how much values bounce around relative to their average, found by dividing the standard deviation by the mean.
kid: One friend usually throws a ball far, another throws it short. To see who is steadier, you compare each one's wobble with how far they usually throw.
detail: The coefficient of variation (CV) is the standard deviation of a set of values divided by their mean, often shown as a percentage. Because it has no units, it compares variability across series of very different sizes: the sales stability of a ₹100 crore firm against a ₹10,000 crore firm, or the swings of two assets per unit of average return. In investing it is sometimes used as risk per unit of return, so a lower CV means less risk for each unit of expected return. It also helps judge earnings stability in credit analysis. Cautions: CV is meaningless when the mean is near zero or negative, because a tiny or negative denominator gives huge or misleading values, so it suits returns poorly when they can average below zero. It also ignores the risk-free rate, which is why the Sharpe ratio is preferred for comparing portfolios.
example: Say fund A has an average annual return of 12% with a standard deviation of 18%, and fund B averages 8% with a standard deviation of 10%. Fund A's CV is 18 / 12 = 1.5 and fund B's is 10 / 8 = 1.25, so B carries less risk per unit of return.

short: A measure of how much an estimate, such as an average calculated from a sample, would likely change if you repeated the sampling.
kid: Tasting one spoon of soup gives you a guess about the whole pot. Tasting many spoons makes your guess much more trustworthy.
detail: The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples, telling you how precise a statistic is. For a sample mean, SE = s / square root of n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the number of observations, so quadrupling the data only halves the error. In finance it is central to judging whether results are real: a fund's average excess return, a regression's alpha or beta, and a backtest's return all have standard errors. A t-statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error; values above about 2 are conventionally treated as significant at the 5% level. Because returns are so volatile, their averages are imprecise even over decades. Confusion to avoid: standard deviation describes the spread of the data, while standard error describes the uncertainty in an estimate made from that data.
example: Say a strategy's monthly returns over 100 months average 0.8% with a standard deviation of 5%. The standard error of the mean is 5% / square root of 100 = 0.5%, so the t-statistic is 0.8 / 0.5 = 1.6, not strong enough to rule out luck at the usual 5% level.
formula: SE of the mean = s / sqrt(n)

short: A way of working out the chances of getting each possible number of successes when you repeat the same yes-or-no try several times.
kid: If you flip a coin four times, you can work out how likely it is to get no heads, one head, two heads and so on. It shows what usually happens.
detail: The binomial distribution gives the probability of k successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same success probability p. Its mean is np and its variance np(1 - p). In finance it models counts of yes-or-no events: how many loans in a pool default, how many trading days close higher, or how many of a manager's calls are right. It underpins the binomial option pricing model, where a stock moves up or down at each step and the number of up-moves after n steps is binomially distributed. It also helps test skill: if a manager beats the benchmark in 9 of 12 months, it tells you how likely that is through luck alone. As n grows it approaches the normal distribution. Confusion to avoid: it assumes independent trials, but defaults and market moves often cluster, so it can badly understate the chance of many failures together.
example: Say a manager beats the market in 9 or more of 12 months. If each month were a 50-50 coin flip, the chance of that is (220 + 66 + 12 + 1) / 4,096 = 299 / 4,096, or about 7.3%, so the record is suggestive but not proof of skill at the usual 5% level.
formula: P(X = k) = C(n, k) x p^k x (1 - p)^(n - k); Mean = n x p; Variance = n x p x (1 - p)

short: A regression problem where two or more explanatory variables move closely together, making it hard to separate their individual effects.
kid: If two friends always push a cart together, you cannot tell who is pushing harder. You only know the cart moved.
detail: Multicollinearity occurs when the explanatory variables in a regression are highly correlated with each other, for example a company's sales and its total assets, or the market return and a large-cap index. The model can still predict well overall, but individual coefficients become unstable: their standard errors balloon, signs can flip with small changes in the data, and genuinely important variables can look insignificant. It is common in factor models and macro forecasting, where many indicators move with the business cycle. Diagnostics include the correlation matrix and the variance inflation factor (VIF), with values above about 5 to 10 usually treated as a warning. Remedies include dropping or combining overlapping variables, using factors built to be uncorrelated, gathering more data, or ridge regression. Confusion to avoid: it concerns correlation among the explanatory variables, not with the variable being explained, and it muddles attribution rather than biasing predictions.
example: Say a model regresses a stock's returns on both the Nifty 50 and the Sensex, whose daily moves are correlated at about 0.99. The fitted betas might come out as 2.1 and -1.0, adding to a sensible 1.1 while each alone is meaningless; with R^2 = 0.99^2 = 0.98 between the two indices, VIF = 1 / (1 - 0.98) = 50.
formula: VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R_j^2), where R_j^2 comes from regressing variable j on the other explanatory variables

short: A situation where the size of random errors or swings in data is not constant but changes over time or across observations.
kid: Some days the sea is calm, and some days the waves are huge. The waves do not stay the same size, and stormy days tend to come in a bunch.
detail: Heteroskedasticity means the variance of a regression's error term is not constant: it changes with the level of an explanatory variable or over time. Its opposite, homoskedasticity, is a standard assumption of ordinary least squares (OLS). When heteroskedasticity is present, OLS coefficients stay unbiased but their usual standard errors are wrong, so t-statistics and significance tests mislead; common fixes are heteroskedasticity-robust (White) standard errors or weighted least squares. In finance it is everywhere: returns are far more volatile in crises such as 2008 and March 2020 than in calm years, and volatility clusters, with big moves following big moves. Robert Engle's ARCH model (1982) and Tim Bollerslev's GARCH extension (1986) model this time-varying volatility for risk management and option pricing; ARCH earned Engle a share of the 2003 economics Nobel. Standard tests include Breusch-Pagan and White. Heteroscedasticity is simply an alternative spelling.
example: Say a stock's daily returns had a standard deviation of 1% in a calm year and 3% in a crisis year. The variance rises from 1 to 9 squared percentage points, a ninefold increase, so a regression assuming one constant variance across both years would report misleading standard errors.
formula: Var(e_i) = sigma_i^2, varying across observations (heteroskedastic), instead of a constant sigma^2 (homoskedastic)

short: Using computer algorithms that learn patterns from data, rather than following hand-written rules, to forecast prices, assess borrowers, detect fraud or trade.
kid: Show a helper thousands of pictures of cats and dogs, and it learns to tell them apart by itself. Computers can learn the same way from lots of examples.
detail: Machine learning (ML) covers methods that learn patterns from data and improve with more examples. In supervised learning, a model learns from labelled examples, such as past loans tagged repaid or defaulted, to predict an outcome; unsupervised learning finds structure, such as clusters of similar stocks, without labels; reinforcement learning improves actions by trial and reward, as in trade execution. Popular tools include decision trees, gradient boosting, neural networks and large language models that read filings and news. Indian banks and NBFCs use ML for credit scoring and fraud detection, and in 2025 an RBI committee published a framework (FREE-AI) for the responsible use of AI in finance. Markets are a hard case: data are noisy, relationships shift and histories are short, so overfitting is the main danger. Confusion to avoid: ML finds correlations, not causes, and a model nobody can explain is hard to trust or justify to regulators.
example: Say a lender trains a model on 1,00,000 past loans, of which 4,000 defaulted, a 4% rate. If the model flags 5,000 new applicants as high risk and 1,000 of them later default, the default rate among flagged loans is 20%, five times the base rate.
